claims.text: Above 900 K, the friction-coefficient spike and loss of wear resistance in FeNiCrCoCu/Cu are driven by SRO dissolution and rapid lattice disordering.
Rapid lattice disordering causes a transition from dislocation-mediated plasticity to amorphous shear banding.
The FeNiCrCoCu coating and Cu matrix are initially single crystals.
At 600 K, the FeNiCrCoCu coating has stable SRO and low dislocation density.
The proposed simulations use 30 Å indentation depth, 10 m/s velocity, and temperatures of 900, 1000, 1100, and 1200 K.
Using vacuum or an inert atmosphere will isolate the target thermal response from oxidation.
Dissolving SRO clusters and emerging amorphous-like regions act as precursors to shear localization.
Above 900 K, thermal energy exceeds the binding energy of SRO configurations in FeNiCrCoCu.
Thermal disordering creates a heterogeneous amorphous phase with low shear strength.
The low-shear-strength amorphous phase facilitates localized shear-band formation.
Localized shear bands act as high-friction interfaces and cause the COF spike.
Loss of crystalline integrity causes catastrophic material removal rather than gradual deformation.
Above 900 K, COF will increase nonlinearly while hardness and wear resistance will drop sharply.
The high-temperature transition will produce a sudden increase in HCP-classified atoms, interpreted as local disordering or FCC-to-HCP-like transformation.
The high-temperature transition will reduce total dislocation line length through dislocation starvation or annihilation within amorphous zones.
At 300 and 600 K, intact SRO and stable or decreasing dislocation density maintain high hardness and low COF.
AlNbTiVZr0.25 has poor oxidation resistance above 600 °C and can disintegrate at 900 °C.
The cited SRO simulation for MoNbTaW assumes a fixed SRO state and neglects ordering or compositional changes around a rapidly moving dislocation.
The SRO-dissolution threshold and the relationship between HCP atom counts and amorphization are unquantified for FeNiCrCoCu.
Comparing dynamically indented samples with a zero-strain-rate thermal-relaxation control using HCP counts, dislocation line length, COF, hardness, and modulus is proposed as the falsification test.
